what: PJT Partners is an advisory firm. It advises companies on mergers and acquisitions, advises companies and creditors through restructurings and bankruptcies, and raises money for private equity and credit funds from institutional investors. It takes no trading positions and lends no money.
customers: Corporate boards and management teams buying or selling businesses, companies in financial distress and the creditor groups negotiating with them, and private fund managers raising capital.
money: Fees for merger advice and for restructuring and liability management work.
Fees for raising capital for private funds and arranging financings.
moat: Advisory businesses are built on individual reputations: a board hires a specific banker, not a firm. PJT’s restructuring practice is among the most respected in the world, and crucially it earns more when markets are bad, which offsets the merger business that earns more when they are good. Having both is a genuinely unusual hedge within one firm.
risks: The business is people, and the people can leave: a departing team takes its client relationships with it, and competitors pay heavily to acquire them.
Merger activity is cyclical and depends on executive confidence and financing availability, neither of which is predictable.
The shares trade at about 19.9 times earnings and 14.9 times EV/EBITDA, which is not cheap for a cyclical fee business.
Only five analysts cover the stock, so the $165.80 average target rests on thin coverage.
Compensation consumes most of the revenue, which limits how much of a strong year reaches shareholders.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year, from $991.9M in 2021 to $1.7B in 2025, through both strong and weak merger markets.
Free cash flow of $688.0M on $1.8B of revenue is remarkable, and the shares trade at about 8.3 times it.
Restructuring and merger advice are countercyclical to each other, which smooths revenue in a way most advisory firms cannot match.
Cash of $538.9M against $413.9M of debt, with no balance sheet risk because the firm takes no positions.
Advisory requires almost no capital, so revenue growth converts to cash rather than being reinvested in assets.
watch: Advisory revenue split between mergers and restructuring. The mix tells you which part of the cycle the firm is earning from, and whether the hedge is working.
view: Advisory firms are among the purest businesses in finance: no balance sheet, no trading positions, no loans, almost no capital required. Revenue arrives as fees for judgement, most of it goes out as compensation, and what remains converts almost entirely to cash. PJT generated $688 million of free cash flow on $1.8 billion of revenue, and the shares trade at about 8.3 times that, which is the sort of number that makes people check the arithmetic.

What makes PJT structurally better than most of its peers is the restructuring practice. Merger advice earns well when executives are confident and financing is cheap; restructuring advice earns well when companies are failing. Owning both inside one firm is a real hedge, and the revenue record demonstrates it — growth every year from $992 million to $1.7 billion, through a merger market that was strong, then frozen, then recovering. Very few advisory firms can show that.

The risk is not financial, it is human, and it is worth taking seriously rather than noting in passing. There is no asset here. A board hires a named banker with a reputation, and if that banker moves to a competitor the revenue follows. Competitors pay enormous sums to acquire exactly these teams. This is why compensation absorbs most of the revenue, and why it will continue to: the firm is in a permanent negotiation with the people who are the firm.

At 19.9 times earnings and 14.9 times EV/EBITDA, the market is pricing a cyclical fee business at a full multiple, and five analysts covering a $5.7 billion company is thin scrutiny for that price. My view is that the countercyclical mix justifies a premium to pure merger advisers and that the quality is real, but the entry price matters more here than in most businesses because the earnings swing with a cycle nobody forecasts well. The mix between merger and restructuring revenue is the most informative disclosure the firm makes, and it is where I would look first every quarter.
bull: The merger and restructuring hedge keeps revenue growing through any market, bankers stay, and 8.3 times free cash flow on a capital-free business proves far too cheap.
bear: A senior team departs with its client relationships, merger activity freezes while restructuring is slow to compensate, and compensation absorbs whatever is left.
